mundra.answer:
IDENTITY PROBLEM FIRST: 4,150 MW and 4,000 MW are both real figures, but neither belongs to the ADANI Mundra plant. Adani Power's own plant page states the Mundra plant has an installed capacity of 4,620 MW in nine units: four 330 MW sub-critical units and five 660 MW supercritical units (4 x 330 + 5 x 660 = 4,620). The 4,150/4,000 pair belongs to the OTHER Mundra coal plant: Tata Power's Coastal Gujarat Power Ltd (CGPL) Mundra Ultra Mega Power Project, which is also the plant at the centre of the IFC/CAO mangrove-and-fisher complaint. If the card is about the port, SEZ and the power plant whose mangrove and fisher harms are documented, the plant is Tata CGPL, not Adani Power's.

FOR THE TATA CGPL MUNDRA UMPP, the two figures ARE different quantities and a document says so. CERC Order in Petition No. 168/MP/2019 (20 June 2025), on CGPL's own petition, states at para 1 that the plant has 'an installed capacity of 4,150 MW (5x830 MW)', and records the petitioner's own evidence at para 6(d) that 'The net plant capacity is 4000 MW (5 units of 800 MW each) after accounting for the Motor Driven Boiler Feed Pump' and that there is a 'maximum gross generation of 830 MW per unit'. Para 17 of the same order: 'Despite each unit being rated for 830 MW, the net plant capacity remains 4,000 MW'. So: 4,150 MW = installed/gross capacity, 5 x 830 MW; 4,000 MW = net plant capacity, 5 x 800 MW net, and also the PPA basis (the order allowed a pass-through 'only on a pro-rata basis for 4,000 MW, rather than the full installed capacity of 4,150 MW'). Tata Power's own Mundra plant page independently gives 'Plant size: 4,150 MW' and 'Five 830 MW "once-through" boilers'. The IFC Summary of Proposed Investment for the Tata Ultra Mega project gives 'a 4,000MW (5 units of 800 MW each) ultra mega imported coal and supercritical technology based power plant', i.e. the net figure.

RECOMMENDATION: if the card means Tata CGPL, carry 4,150 MW installed (5 x 830 MW) with 4,000 MW net, both attributed, citing the CERC order as the document that distinguishes them. If the card means Adani Power's Mundra plant, both figures on the card are wrong and the figure is 4,620 MW (4 x 330 + 5 x 660).

shuakhevi.answer:
185 MW DOES have sources - IFC's own - so it is not an invented number, but IFC's documents are internally inconsistent and nothing reconciles 185 with 184.

What each figure covers, from IFC project 33435 (Adjaristsqali Georgia LLC / Georgia CEI HPP):
- 184 MW = the financed project as a whole. IFC's Summary of Investment Information: 'the 184 MW Shuakhevi hydropower project' and 'consisting of 2 HPP schemes: the 178 MW Shuakhevi HPP and the 6 MW Skhalta HPP'. IFC's ESRS: 'The proposed investment is a 184 MW hydropower scheme comprised of two dams'.
- 178 MW = the Shuakhevi HPP powerhouse alone. IFC ESRS: 'a 18 km tunnel from the Didachara reservoir to the 178 MW Shuakhevi HPP.'
- 6 MW = the Skhalta HPP. IFC ESRS: 'a 6.4 km tunnel from the Chirukhistskali River through to a 6 MW Hydro Power Plant (HPP) on the Skhalta river'.
- 185 MW = IFC's figure for 'the Shuakhevi scheme' as one of the three schemes in the Adjaristsqali cascade. IFC Early Disclosure for project 33435 (disclosed 24 May 2013): 'The project consists of financing the 185 MW hydro power plant in Adjaritskali, southwest Georgia', '(Shuakhevi 185MW, Koromkheti 150MW, and Khertvisi 65MW)' and 'IFC is considering to invest in the first HPP (Shuakhevi 185 MW) of the three HPPs.' The SAME IFC ESRS that gives 178 MW and 184 MW in its project description also writes, in its cascade description, 'namely the 185 MW Shuakhevi scheme, the 150 MW Koromkheti scheme and the 65 MW Khertvisi scheme'. CEE Bankwatch Network's project briefing likewise says 'for the construction of the 185 MW Shuakhevi hydropower plant (HPP)'.
- A fourth figure exists: ADB's own press release says 'The project will develop the 187-megawatt Shuakhevi hydropower scheme' 'consisting of the Shuakhevi and Skhalta hydropower plants'.

No document explains the gap between 185 and 184, or 187. 178 + 6 = 184 is arithmetic IFC itself performs in print, so 184 MW is the best-attested figure for the financed Shuakhevi + Skhalta project, and that is what I would put on the card: '184 MW (Shuakhevi 178 MW plus Skhalta 6 MW), per IFC; IFC's 2013 early disclosure and its ESRS cascade description give 185 MW for the Shuakhevi scheme and ADB gives 187 MW.' The card's bare 185 MW is sourced but is IFC's earlier, pre-appraisal figure and does not match the configuration IFC later financed.

antea.answer:
It is a plain disagreement, and it is not even a disagreement between Titan and IFC - it is internal to IFC's own disclosure package for project 25886 (Antea Albania), and both figures are expressly for CEMENT, both describing output from the same 3,300 tonnes-per-day clinker line.

- IFC Summary of Proposed Investment, disclosed 26 March 2008: 'a production capacity of 3300 tons per day clinker (or 1,400,000tons per year cement)'. The page says only 'production capacity'; it does not call this design, nameplate or permitted capacity.
- IFC Environmental and Social Review Summary for the same project: the plant is 'capable of producing a total of 1.50 Million tons cement per year near Fushe Kruje', and in the greenhouse-gas section, 'the final CO2 emissions from a production of up to 1.50 million tons of cement per year will be 975,000 tons CO2.' The same ESRS describes the facility as 'a 3,300 tpd clinker production facility' - the identical clinker line.

So the clinker/cement confusion that normally explains a 1.4-vs-1.5 gap is NOT what is happening here: both numbers are cement, and both sit beside the same 3,300 tpd clinker figure. Neither document labels its figure design, achieved or permitted, and no document I opened distinguishes them. I did not find any source that says one figure is design capacity and the other permitted or achieved output, so I am not offering that explanation.

The card should give both, attributed: '1.5 million tonnes of cement a year (Titan; also IFC's Environmental and Social Review Summary) / 1.4 million tonnes of cement a year (IFC Summary of Proposed Investment, March 2008)', from a 3,300 tonnes-per-day clinker line (both documents).

NOTE ON ATTRIBUTION: I could not open Titan's own pages. titanmaterials.com (to which titan-cement.com now 302-redirects) returned PROVENANCE_REQUIRED on both the 2022 Albania integrated annual report PDF and the Antea plant page - a permission request that went unanswered, NOT the host refusing. The 1.5 Mt figure does not depend on that, because IFC's own ESRS states it twice.

huaneng_shandong_ruyi.answer:
UNSOURCED, and the split as the card states it is contradicted at the level the card puts it.

The 51/49 traces to exactly one place and stops there. AidData's own project record (project 52659, the Sahiwal 1,320 MW / 2 x 660 MW plant) describes Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Pakistan) Energy Ltd as a 'joint venture of Huaneng Shandong Power Generation Co. Ltd. (51% ownership stake)' and 'Shandong Ruyi Science & Technology Group (49% ownership stake)' - and cites no source for those percentages. AidData's staff comments link sources for the sovereign guarantee, the debt pricing and the repayment terms, but none of them for the shareholding.

Against it, a regulated credit rating agency says the Pakistani project company has a single shareholder. PACRA's rating report on the company states: 'It is a wholly owned subsidiary of Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Hong Kong) Energy Limited, a company incorporated in Hong Kong' and 'The ultimate parent of the Company is China Huaneng Group Company Limited.' So if any 51/49 split exists it would sit at the Hong Kong holding company, not at the project company the card names.

And at the Hong Kong holding company, the only percentages I could open give a different pair: Global Energy Monitor's Global Energy Ownership Tracker record for Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Hong Kong) Energy Ltd (statement gem-own-e100002007872, dated 30 June 2024) lists Huaneng Shandong Power Generation at 50.00% and Jining Chengtou Holding Group at 50.00% - Shandong Ruyi does not appear at all.

NEPRA documents name the sponsors without percentages. GEM's Sahiwal power station page gives 'Sponsor: Huaneng Shandong Electricity and Shandong Ruyi Group' and 'Parent company: China Huaneng Group and Shandong Ruyi Group' with no figures, and cites Dawn (21 April 2015) and The International News (7 July 2015) for consortium membership only.

RECOMMENDATION: drop the percentages. The card can say the project company is a joint venture of Huaneng Shandong Power Generation (China Huaneng Group) and Shandong Ruyi Science and Technology Group, held through Huaneng Shandong Ruyi (Hong Kong) Energy Ltd, with no published split.

kepco_spc.answer:
SOURCED, but from Philippine newspaper reporting rather than a filing, and only KEPCO's 60% is stated outright.

KEPCO's 60%: The Philippine Star, 19 January 2023, reports that 'KEPCO is in the process of selling its 60 percent stake in KEPCO SPC Power Corp. (KSPC)'. The same article describes KSPC only as 'a joint venture between KEPCO and SPC Power' without giving SPC's figure.

SPC's 40%: The Philippine Star, 21 October 2007, reporting the formation of the Cebu joint venture, says of Salcon Power Corp. (SPC) that 'the company will invest 40 percent in the project' and that '60 percent of the total capitalization of the project will be provided by Kephilco'. The article's own wording presents these as the split of project investment and capitalisation, not explicitly as shareholding in the joint venture company, and it names the Korean partner 'Kepco Philippines Corp. (Kephilco)'.

No filing states it. I could not find the split in any SPC Power Corporation disclosure: the SEC Form 17-A / PSE Disclosure Form 17-1 for the year ended 31 December 2018 (PSE Edge file 573067) does not mention KSPC or KEPCO at all; SPC's Public Ownership Report for 30 September 2026 and its List of Top 100 Stockholders for the same period give only percentages of SPC itself (notably KEPCO Philippines Holdings, Inc. at 37.96% of SPC Power Corporation - a different shareholding that is easy to confuse with the JV stake). KEPCO Philippines' own Cebu CFBC Power Plant page calls KSPC 'a joint venture of KEPCO Philippines, Holdings, Inc. and SPC Power Corporation' with no percentages. KEPCO's SEC Form 20-F for FY2023 is 4.07 million characters; the first 100,000 contain no mention of KSPC and I did not page through the remaining 3.97 million.

Beware one trap: Global Energy Monitor's Naga power complex page gives a REVERSED pair - 'originally owned by SPC Power Corp., a subsidiary of Salcon Power (60%) and Korea Electric Power Company (KEPCO) (40%)' - but that sentence is about the original Naga-1 plant and the ownership of SPC Power Corp., not about KSPC, and GEM attaches no citation to it.

RECOMMENDATION: the card's 60/40 can stand if it is attributed to news reporting - '60% KEPCO, 40% SPC Power (Philippine Star, 2007 and 2023)' - and the card should not imply a filing supports it.

iso_tech.answer:
The 4% IS sourced - but the source that carries it gives a three-way structure that does not match the card's '96% PowerChina / 4% Iso Tech'.

The 4% appears in two places that open:
- AidData's project record 71614 describes Barisal Electric Power Company Ltd as 'a special purpose vehicle and joint venture of' 'Barisal Energy (DFC) Holding Limited (92% ownership stake)', 'Sinohydro (Hong Kong) Holdings Limited (4% ownership stake)' and 'ISO Tech Electrification Company Limited (4% ownership stake)'. AidData cites no source for these percentages.
- EnergyTransitionBD (the Bangladesh Working Group on External Debt's project database) states for Unit 1 that 'BEDICL invested $149.04 million, while ITECL and SHKHL invested $6.48 million each', 'holding 92%, 4%, and 4% share of the project', and cites PowerChina's own press release at pr.powerchina.cn/2434.html for the figures. BWGED's own Barisal factsheet lists 'Sponsor: SHKHL (Sinohydro (Hong Kong) Holdings Limited): 4%' and 'Sponsor: ISO Tech Electrification Company Limited: 4%'.

Against that, Global Energy Monitor's Barisal power station page says only 'PowerChina owns 96% of the shares', citing the Land Portal / Eco-Business report 'China builds coal power plant in Bangladesh despite protests' (29 April 2021) and PowerChina's own subsidiaries listing. The Eco-Business version of that article, which I opened, says 'PowerChina owns 96 per cent of the shares' and names ISO Tech Electrification Company Limited as the Bangladeshi partner without giving it a percentage. So Iso Tech's 4% on the card is not derived from that source - it is a residual.

No document I opened reconciles '96% PowerChina' with '92% / 4% / 4%'. The two structures name different shareholders at different levels, and I am not going to supply the bridge.

RECOMMENDATION: give the structure as published rather than the pair. '92% Barisal Energy (DFC) Holding Ltd, 4% Sinohydro (Hong Kong) Holdings Ltd, 4% ISO Tech Electrification Company Ltd (AidData; BWGED/EnergyTransitionBD, citing PowerChina), with Global Energy Monitor reporting that PowerChina owns 96% of the shares.' On that basis Iso Tech's 4% stands, and it is the 96%-as-a-single-shareholding that should carry the caveat.

BLOCKED: PowerChina's own press release at https://pr.powerchina.cn/2434.html - the primary source BWGED cites for 92/4/4 - returned PROVENANCE_REQUIRED, an unanswered permission request, NOT the host refusing. It is worth one retry in a session where permissions are being answered; it would settle this outright.
